Regarding the definition of "zero-shot generalization" in the context of text-to-image AIs, it seems sensible. The concept of zero-shot generalization refers to the ability of a model to apply its learned knowledge to new, unseen concepts without requiring additional training data. In the context of text-to-image AIs, this means that the model can generate images based on text prompts without having seen the specific images or concepts before.

The 2013 paper that defines zero-shot generalization likely refers to the work of Fei-Fei Li, a computer scientist and director of the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Lab (SAIL). Li has been a prominent researcher in the field of artificial intelligence, particularly in the areas of computer vision and natural language processing.

In the context of text-to-image AIs, zero-shot generalization is an important capability, as it enables the model to generate a wide range of images based on a limited set of text prompts. This has potential applications in areas such as image generation, image-to-image translation, and image-based storytelling.

However, it's worth noting that zero-shot generalization is a challenging problem, and achieving it requires a deep understanding of the underlying concepts and relationships between text and images. Researchers continue to explore new approaches and techniques to improve the performance of text-to-image AIs and enable them to generalize to new, unseen concepts.
